title: Waterfall and iterative-incremental delivery
blurb: Contrast waterfall with iterative-incremental delivery and name the three PRINCE2 Agile timeboxes.
question: A project manager plans a stage containing two releases, each made of three iterations. What is the main advantage of this over a single waterfall sequence, and which of these timeboxes is the largest?

teach.body: The PRINCE2 Agile glossary defines waterfall as linear sequential delivery. Each phase, such as requirements, design, build and test, must be fully complete before the next begins. The book names its main limitation: waterfall does not allow for adaptability during the process. Users typically see the finished product only at the end, when change is hardest and most expensive.

Iterative means working in repeated short cycles, refining the product as you learn. Incremental means delivering it in usable pieces, each adding to the last. Together they bring value and feedback early and often. PRINCE2 Project Management can host any delivery method, linear-sequential or iterative-incremental, but PRINCE2 Agile is specifically for iterative and incremental (agile) delivery.

teach.h: Timeboxes: fix the time, flex the content
teach.body: A timebox is a fixed period of time in which work is done. PRINCE2 Agile uses three levels: the iteration (the shortest, where a team builds an increment), the release (usually two to four iterations, delivering something usable) and the stage (the management stage the board authorizes). When time runs out, the timebox ends; what flexes is how much is delivered.

Bramblewood Council's first plan for a new parking-permit service was nine months of specification and build, with residents seeing nothing until go-live. Project manager Grace Okafor replans with PRINCE2 Agile: one stage holding two releases of three two-week iterations. Release 1 lets existing permit holders renew online. Their feedback reshapes the priorities for release 2.

teach.text: Iterative-incremental does not mean 'no plan' or 'no stages'. PRINCE2 Agile keeps management stages as the largest timebox, with releases and iterations inside them. And a release is bigger than an iteration, not the other way round.

items: Waterfall: linear sequential; each phase complete before the next; main limitation is no adaptability during the process.
Iterative-incremental: repeated cycles delivering usable increments, so value and feedback come early.
PRINCE2 Agile is specifically for iterative-incremental delivery.
Three timeboxes: iteration, release (usually 2 to 4 iterations) and stage.

summary: You can now contrast waterfall with iterative-incremental delivery and explain why early, frequent increments help. You can also name the three PRINCE2 Agile timeboxes and place them in order of size.

A.q: How does the PRINCE2 Agile glossary describe waterfall?
A.why: The glossary defines waterfall as linear sequential delivery: each phase is completed before the next starts.

whyNot.0: Iterative and incremental delivery is the agile alternative to waterfall.
whyNot.1: Flow with work-in-progress limits describes Kanban.
whyNot.3: Timeboxed sprints describe Scrum, an agile approach.

A.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, what is the main limitation of waterfall delivery?
options: It does not allow adaptability during the process
It cannot be governed through a project board
It needs delivery teams that manage themselves
It releases too many early versions to users
A.why: The book says the main limitation of waterfall is that it does not allow adaptability during the process (2.2).

whyNot.1: Waterfall projects can be governed by a project board; that is not its limitation.
whyNot.2: Self-management is an agile idea, not a waterfall requirement.
whyNot.3: Waterfall typically delivers once, at the end, not in many early versions.

A.q: What are the three levels of timebox in PRINCE2 Agile?
A.why: The glossary names three timebox levels: iteration, release and stage.

whyNot.0: An epic is a large user story, not a timebox.
whyNot.1: A task is a unit of work inside an iteration, not one of the three timebox levels.
whyNot.2: An increment is the product delivered, and the project is not named as a timebox level.

B.q: How many iterations does a release usually contain in PRINCE2 Agile?
B.why: A release usually spans two to four iterations (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: A release normally contains more than one or two iterations; the usual range is two to four.
whyNot.2: Five to seven is longer than the usual release of two to four iterations.
whyNot.3: Eight to ten iterations would be unusually long for a single release.

B.q: Which delivery approach is PRINCE2 Agile specifically designed for?
B.why: PRINCE2 Project Management can host any delivery method, but PRINCE2 Agile is specifically for iterative and incremental delivery (1.3.4).

whyNot.0: Linear-sequential delivery can be governed by PRINCE2 Project Management, but it is not what PRINCE2 Agile is for.
whyNot.1: Waterfall with fixed scope is the opposite of agile's flexible scope.
whyNot.2: A single handover at the end is a waterfall pattern.

options: Delivering the product in usable pieces over time
Completing each phase before starting the next
Delivering the whole product at the very end
Fixing all requirements before design starts
B.why: Incremental delivery builds and delivers the product in usable pieces, each adding to what is already there.

whyNot.1: Completing phases in sequence describes waterfall.
whyNot.2: A single delivery at the end is typical of waterfall.
whyNot.3: Fixing every requirement up front is a waterfall habit, not what incremental means.

C.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. In waterfall, each phase is completed before the next one starts.
2. A timebox has a fixed end; the amount delivered can flex.
3. A release is a shorter timebox than an iteration.
4. Iterative-incremental delivery postpones user feedback until the end.
C.why: Waterfall completes each phase in turn (1), and a timebox fixes time while the content flexes (2).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is wrong: a release usually contains two to four iterations, so it is longer.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: iterative-incremental delivery brings feedback early and often.
whyNot.3: Both are wrong: releases are longer than iterations, and feedback comes early.

C.q: A project manager plans a stage containing two releases of three iterations each. Which statement about these timeboxes is correct?
options: The stage contains releases, which contain iterations
The release contains the stage and its iterations
The iterations run outside the management stage
C.why: The stage is the largest timebox; it contains releases, and each release usually contains two to four iterations.

whyNot.0: This reverses the order: releases contain iterations, not the other way round.
whyNot.2: The stage is the largest of the three timeboxes, so a release sits inside it.
whyNot.3: Iterations take place within the stage the board has authorized.

C.q: In traditional projects, when is product quality typically assessed, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
options: At the end of each iteration
C.why: Table 2.2 lists late assessment of quality as a problem of traditional projects, causing missed chances to fix issues early.

whyNot.1: Checking quality every iteration is the agile response to this problem.
whyNot.2: Stand-ups are an agile event and are not where traditional projects assess quality.
whyNot.3: Quality cannot be assessed before requirements exist; the problem is that it happens late.

reteach.title: One big meal or a series of courses
reteach.question: Why do frequent increments beat one big delivery when needs are uncertain?

blocks.body: Waterfall is like cooking a whole banquet and serving it all at once: if the guests dislike the main dish, it is too late. Iterative-incremental delivery serves course by course and asks the guests after each one, so the next course can change. The meal still has a fixed time slot (the timebox); what changes is what gets served in it.

test.q: What is the main advantage of iterative-incremental delivery over waterfall?
options: Every requirement is fixed before work starts
Value and feedback arrive early and often
Testing happens once, in a single final phase
No planning is needed before starting
test.why: Delivering in repeated cycles of usable increments brings value and feedback early, so the product can adapt.

whyNot.0: Fixing every requirement up front is a waterfall feature.
whyNot.2: A single final test phase is how waterfall assesses quality late.
whyNot.3: Agile still plans, just in time and at several levels.

test.why: The iteration is the shortest timebox; releases contain iterations and stages contain releases.

whyNot.0: The stage is the largest timebox.
whyNot.1: A release usually contains two to four iterations.
whyNot.3: An increment is what an iteration produces, not a timebox.
